problem: The pull-in condition is stated backwards. For a linear spring the instability occurs when the plate has moved one third of the initial gap, so the remaining gap is two thirds of the initial gap, not one third.
fix: As the plate moves, g falls and F rises as 1/g². The spring force rises linearly with displacement x = g0 − g. Beyond x = g0/3 (remaining gap 2g0/3) the electrostatic force grows faster than the spring can balance and the plates snap together; a simple voltage control cannot hold a stable position past that point.

problem: Step 5 uses the wrong pull-in rule: g/3 = 0.667 µm. With g0 = 2 µm the plate pulls in after moving 1/3 of the gap, leaving 2/3 of the gap.
fix: step 5: Pull-in occurs when the plate has moved one third of the initial gap: displacement = g0/3 = (2 µm)/3 = 0.667 µm, so the remaining gap is 2g0/3 = 1.33 µm. answer: capacitance ≈ 0.177 pF, force ≈ 39.8 µN, and pull-in occurs after 0.667 µm of travel, at a remaining gap of about 1.33 µm.

problem: Trap says pull-in is at one third of the initial gap, not half. Wrong number: pull-in displacement is one third; the remaining gap at pull-in is two thirds.
fix: Pull-in occurs after the plate has moved one third of the initial gap, so the remaining gap is two thirds of the initial gap (not half); beyond that displacement voltage control is unstable.

problem: The answer states the threshold as 'past g/3', i.e. remaining gap one third, which contradicts the standard pull-in result.
fix: As the gap falls, electrostatic force rises as 1/g² while the spring force rises linearly with displacement. Past a displacement of g0/3 (remaining gap 2g0/3) the electrostatic force grows faster, so any small further movement increases force more than the spring can balance; the plates snap together.

problem: The figure states 'pull-in at g/3' and 'pull-in at one third of the gap', which is the wrong threshold.
fix: Use note 'pull-in after g/3 travel' or 'pull-in at 2g/3 remaining gap', and aria text 'electrostatic, with pull-in after one third of the gap is travelled'.

problem: 'The force is the derivative of energy with gap' is loose: at constant voltage the force is +∂U/∂x (the source supplies work); at constant charge it is −∂U/∂x. Students meeting this for the first time can get the sign wrong.
fix: At constant applied voltage the force is +∂U/∂x with x measured along the closing direction, which gives the ε0AV²/(2g²) formula; at constant charge the sign flips but the magnitude is the same.
